transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-08-30 15:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Priya Menon (Redwood SE), Sam Lee (Apex CTO), Maria Gomez (Apex Product), Ethan Cho (Apex SRE)

Summary:
Quick product walkthrough focused on structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool-calling. Covered console schema guardrails, API examples, and Redwood Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization. Discussed security (SOC2, KMS, VPC) and next steps for a pilot and benchmark.

Topics: Structured output, JSON mode, schema enforcement, function calling, tool calling, console demo, guardrails, Optimize recommendations, Dedicated vs Hosted, security & data residency.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan Park from Redwood, quick intros?
[01:00] Sam (Apex): Sam Lee here, CTO, Maria product, Ethan SRE. We're excited to see how structured outputs could reduce our post-processing work.
[02:00] Priya (Redwood): Great, Priya from Redwood infra team, I'll drive the demo, focus on JSON mode and function/tool calls.
[03:00] Maria (Apex): Quick note, our primary constraints: sub-200ms p99 for short inference, data residency in us-east, and SOC2 compliance.
[04:00] Jordan: Perfect, we'll show both hosted and Dedicated flavors, and how the console enforces schemas so you don't get back a malformed JSON.
[05:00] Priya: I'll start with the API flow — JSON mode supports a schema param, you can provide a JSON Schema or a shorthand template. We validate at runtime and send structured payloads back.
[06:00] Sam: So is that the same as the function calling we saw in some other vendors?
[07:00] Priya: Similar idea, yes, but Redwood's has both function and tool calling; tool calling is for external actions like hitting your microservice and function calling is the model returning arguments. We also have guardrails in the console to prevent schema drift.
[08:00] Ethan (Apex): How does fallback work if the model can't match the schema? We need predictable behavior.
[09:00] Priya: Good question — you can set strict/loose modes. In strict mode the runtime returns an error and optionally a best-effort partial object. In loose mode it will attempt to coerce types. We also let you set fallback to a different model variant or route to a canary.
[10:00] Maria: Can you show the console? I'd like to see the schema UI and guardrails.
[11:00] Priya: Yep, sharing my screen now — this is the Redwood Console, go to Routes -> JSON Mode. Here you can upload a JSON Schema, map fields, and set required fields.
[12:00] Jordan: Note that the console also ties these schemas to rollouts, so you can do a canary with a relaxed schema and then lock it down on full rollout.
[13:00] Sam: Can we add custom validation? Like regex for SKU formats?
[14:00] Priya: Yes, you can add custom validators and custom error messages. We also record validation failures in the trace logs so you can inspect them in the Console Diagnostics tab.
[15:00] Ethan: About performance — does schema enforcement add latency?
[16:00] Priya: Minimal, it's essentially a validation step. The heavy parts are still the model inference and KV cache lookups. We optimize validation in native code paths, it's usually single-digit milliseconds. In Dedicated mode you can pin quantized variants for even lower latencies.
[17:00] Sam: Show us an example with function calling and an external tool.
[18:00] Priya: Sure — demo time. I'm calling the API endpoint here: POST /v1/generate with mode=json and a schema. Then I include tool definitions — e.g., an inventory check tool with an openapi-ish spec.
[19:00] Maria: The tool calling, does Redwood run the tool or is it a mocked interface?
[20:00] Priya: You provide the tool integration; Redwood can host adapters or you can call the tool from your infra. In hosted mode we offer secure outbound connectors; in private/Dedicated you run the connector inside your VPC.
[21:00] Jordan: Important for compliance: outbound connectors can be configured to use customer-managed keys and egress controls.
[22:00] Sam: What about KV cache? We rely heavily on prefix caching for conversational state.
[23:00] Priya: The KV cache supports pinned prefixes and TTLs; we surface hit/miss rates in Optimize so you can tune. Also automatic prefix caching can reduce token usage significantly.
[24:00] Ethan: Any gotchas with quantized models and schema fidelity? We've seen hallucinations increase after 4-bit quant.
[25:00] Priya: Right, that's where Redwood Optimize comes in — it recommends quantization levels per workload. For structured output we often suggest keeping certain layers in fp16 or using a 6-bit profile. You can also set quality monitors tied to prompt sets to catch regressions.
[26:00] Maria: Could you show the test harness? We want to run our sample SKUs through it.
[27:00] Priya: I'm switching to the Evals tab — you can upload a prompt set and expected JSON outputs; Redwood will run diffs and surface schema mismatches and ROC-like metrics for fields.
[28:00] Sam: Nice, can it run at scale? We want to baseline at 1k requests per second.
[29:00] Priya: For benchmarking we usually spin up a Dedicated pool and provide a benchmark spreadsheet. We'll run a baseline with the sample payloads and share latency/cost per 1k TPS.
[30:00] Jordan: We'll include both hosted (burst) and Dedicated configurations so you see tradeoffs.
[31:00] Ethan: Security questions — SOC2, SAML SSO, audit logs, KMS.
[32:00] Jordan: Redwood is SOC2 Type II, we support SAML and SCIM for provisioning, RBAC in the Console, and you can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key control in Private deployments. Audit logs are available via the Console and streaming to your syslog/S3.
[33:00] Maria: Data residency — we need data to stay in us-east for at-rest and in-transit.
[34:00] Jordan: We offer region pinning and Private deployments for strict residency. For hosted we have region-specific endpoints and retention policies. We'll share the policy doc after the call.
[35:00] Sam: Back to function calling — how does Redwood handle multi-step tool workflows? For example, call inventory service then pricing service.
[36:00] Priya: You can chain tools and define orchestration in the console or via a small state machine. We also capture tool outputs in the trace so you can replay or audit. There's optional signing for tool calls.
[37:00] Ethan: Replayability is key for debugging — can we get full request/response traces including intermediate tool outputs?
[38:00] Priya: Yes, traces include prompt, model selection, schema validation events, tool invocation payloads, and timing. You can export traces for compliance reviews.
[39:00] Maria: Any mention of cost? We need an estimate of tokens + tool call overhead.
[40:00] Jordan: We'll send a pilot pricing sheet. For structured outputs token usage tends to be lower because you avoid freeform text post-processing, but tool calls and outbound connectors are billed separately. We'll include estimated unit economics in the spreadsheet.
[41:00] Sam: Competitor question — we've looked at Anthropic's approach and some vendors that only do function calling. What's Redwood's advantage?
[42:00] Priya: Our differentiator is the production-grade runtime + Console guardrails + Optimize tooling. You get predictable latency, caching, and rollout controls that are designed for ops teams.
[43:00] Ethan: Can we do an on-prem or VPC install? Some workloads need full air-gap or private control plane.
[44:00] Jordan: Yes — Private includes a customer-managed control plane and on-prem package; Dedicated is reserved capacity but still managed by Redwood. We'll map options in the proposal.
[45:00] Maria: Show me the sample code for SDK usage in Node — how simple is it to call JSON mode?
[46:00] Priya: Quick example — pass schema parameter, mode: 'json', and tools. The SDK will surface typed responses if you provide a schema so your app gets native JSON objects instead of parsing strings.
[47:00] Sam: What happens when model output violates schema in production? We need alerts.
[48:00] Priya: We have quality monitors in Optimize — set thresholds for field-level accuracy, and you'll get regression alerts. You can also autopurge bad responses or flag them for manual review.
[49:00] Ethan: For the pilot, we'll want a Dedicated pool with a canary policy and a runbook for failover.
[50:00] Jordan: We'll include a canary + auto-fallback plan in the pilot doc. Also suggest a caching policy and batching windows to meet your p99 target economically.
[51:00] Maria: Any caveats with streaming structured output? We want some streaming for big payloads.
[52:00] Priya: Streaming is supported but schema validation completes at the end; for streaming you can stream partial objects or use a chunked schema mode. There's a small tradeoff in validation latency but it's manageable.
[53:00] Sam: Great. Let's summarize next steps.
[54:00] Jordan: Recap: Jordan to send pricing and pilot options; Priya to run baseline benchmark with sample payloads; Ethan to share payloads and residency requirements; schedule follow-up benchmark call next week.
